Where is Manchester and how is it laid out?

Manchester sits in south-central New Hampshire on the Merrimack River, about 20 miles from the Massachusetts border and 58 miles from Boston. It is in Hillsborough County, which shares its county seat role between Manchester and Nashua.

Wikipedia, citing Census figures, lists the city at 34.93 square miles in total, with 33.07 of that land and 1.87 water. The 2020 Census counted 115,644 residents. The city's 2010 Master Plan divides it into 25 neighborhoods, and that matters for a tax guide because assessments and house styles change a lot from one to the next.

  • West Side: Amoskeag, Rimmon Heights, Notre Dame/McGregorville, and Piscataquog/Granite Square
  • East Side: North End, Janeville/Corey Square, Hallsville, and Bakersville
  • Outer areas: Youngsville and Goffes Falls

Someone selling a house on the West Side may deal with the same Board of Assessors and Tax Collector as someone selling in Goffes Falls, but the buyer pool and the age of the housing can look very different.

How did Manchester become a mill city?

Manchester was granted as Tyngstown in 1727, chartered as Derryfield in 1751, renamed Manchester in 1810, and incorporated as a city in 1846. The name change came the same year the Amoskeag Cotton & Woolen Manufacturing Company was incorporated, and the mills defined the city for the next century.

The Amoskeag company's Mill No. 11 was 900 feet long and held about 4,000 looms. The company town on the east bank was founded in 1838, with Elm Street as its main road. About 17,000 workers from Amoskeag and Stark struck for nine months in 1922, and Amoskeag went bankrupt in 1935. The Great Flood of 1936 then hit the Merrimack valley and destroyed the McGregor Bridge.

The city's own area profile says downtown development now centers on revitalized mill buildings along the river. For a seller, the practical point is age: the city's housing stock is older than most, and an older house is more likely to need work before it shows well.

What do people in Manchester do for work?

Health care, higher education, utilities and finance are the largest employer groups listed for the Manchester area. The table below shows the largest employers in a 2017 list reproduced on Wikipedia, so treat the headcounts as dated.

EmployerEmployees (2017, Manchester ZIP area)
Elliot Hospital3,682
Catholic Medical Center2,600
Southern New Hampshire University2,093
Eversource Energy1,400
FairPoint Communications1,050

More than 8,000 students attend the city's colleges and universities, which include Manchester Community College, the University of New Hampshire at Manchester, and Southern New Hampshire University. The airport, SNHU Arena and the Fisher Cats ballpark round out the list of large facilities the city names in its profile. Roughly half of Manchester's occupied homes are rented, so a sale often involves a house with tenants or a landlord who owns more than one property.

How do roads, the airport and the weather affect a Manchester house?

Interstates 93 and 293, the F.E. Everett Turnpike, and NH Routes 101, 3 and 3A serve the city, and Manchester-Boston Regional Airport is the fourth-largest passenger airport in New England. Commuters to Boston and Concord are a real part of the buyer pool.

The weather is a larger factor in condition than location. Wikipedia lists a mean January temperature of 25.6 degrees Fahrenheit and a July mean of 73.8 degrees, with about 40 inches of precipitation a year. The Merrimack River, the Piscataquog River and Cohas Brook all run through or beside the city, and the 1936 flood remains the best-known example of what the river can do.

  • Older roofs and chimneys take freeze and thaw cycles every year.
  • Heating systems in 1960s houses are often original or near the end of their life.
  • Homes near the rivers and brook deserve a look at the basement and the flood zone status before listing.

A cash buyer prices these items in directly, which is why many Manchester owners with deferred repairs choose an as-is sale.

How does Manchester property tax work?

Manchester's property tax year runs April 1 to March 31 under RSA 76:2, and taxes are assessed on the inventory taken that April. The Board of Assessors sets the value, and the Office of the Tax Collector bills it.

The Assessors explain that value is estimated three ways: recent sales of comparable properties, replacement cost less depreciation, and, for income property such as apartments, an income approach. The tax rate is the levy divided by total assessed value, and the same rate applies to every owner. The state Department of Revenue Administration issues the rate in October or November.

Bills go out twice a year. The first, mailed in early June, is based on half of the previous year's rate. The second, mailed in late November, uses the new rate and any assessment changes. Each bill is due 30 days after it is issued. The city's real estate page lists a 2025 rate of 20.24 per $1,000, up from 19.58 for 2024, and a separate Central Business Service District rate of 0.462730 for 2025.

What happens if Manchester property tax goes unpaid?

Unpaid Manchester tax moves from interest to a lien in about a year and can end in a city tax deed after two years. The steps below come from the Tax Collector's real estate process page and the cited statutes.

StepWhat the city says
Interest8 percent per year on late taxes (RSA 76:13)
Notice of ArrearageSent about 30 days after each billing (RSA 76:11-b)
Notice of Impending LienCertified mail at least 30 days before the lien is executed (RSA 80:60)
Lien executedInterest becomes 14 percent per year (RSA 80:69); lien recorded at the Registry of Deeds within 30 days
Mortgagee noticeSent 60 days after execution, with a $10 fee plus any title search cost (RSA 80:67)
Tax deedIf unpaid two years after execution, with a notice of impending deed at least 30 days earlier (RSA 80:76, 80:77)

After a deed, a prior owner or mortgagee who wants to reclaim the property must notify the city by certified mail within 30 days of the notice of intent to repurchase. They have to show they can pay the back taxes, interest, costs and a penalty of 10 percent of the equalized assessed value (RSA 80:89).

How do you challenge a Manchester assessment?

Send a written abatement application to the Board of Assessors so that it is received or postmarked by March 1 after the final tax bill. The city says it cannot be filed online because an original signature is required, and there is no filing fee with the city.

You must be the owner of record on April 1 of the tax year, or otherwise an aggrieved party, and you carry the burden of showing the property was assessed disproportionately compared with other property in town. The Board has until July 1 to decide. If it says nothing by then, the application is treated as denied.

  • Further appeal is due by September 1.
  • Choose one route: the State Board of Tax and Land Appeals (written, with a fee) or Hillsborough County Superior Court, Northern District, 300 Chestnut Street, Manchester.
  • Filing with the Board of Tax and Land Appeals waives the right to petition the Superior Court (RSA 76-B:11).

If you are selling and think the value is wrong, mention the pending application to the title company, since the outcome affects the tax bill for the year you owned the house.

How do you sell a Manchester house with property tax still due?

Tell the title company at the start, because unpaid tax and any recorded lien are paid out of the sale proceeds at closing. The Tax Collector can provide a copy of a lien release for $10 per property plus $2 per receipt requested, by email at Taxcollector@manchesternh.gov or in person at One City Hall Plaza.

Redeemed liens are released within 30 days, and the release is mailed to the Hillsborough County Register of Deeds, 19 Temple Street, Nashua. The Assessors also warn that a new deed can take 30 days or more to reach their office, so the bill may still carry the seller's name after closing. Pass new-owner and address information along in writing.

New Hampshire's real estate transfer tax is $0.75 per $100 of the price, paid by both the buyer and the seller, with a $20 minimum each when the price is $4,000 or less. Stamps are bought from the register of deeds, and the Purchaser's and Seller's Declarations of Consideration (CD-57-P and CD-57-S) and the PA-34 inventory are due to the state within 30 days after the deed is recorded.

More questions about Manchester, NH Property Tax Guide

When is Manchester property tax due?

Two bills a year, each due 30 days after it is issued. The first goes out in early June and the second in late November, according to the Tax Collector. The tax year runs April 1 to March 31.

What is the interest rate on late Manchester property tax?

8 percent per year on unpaid taxes under RSA 76:13. Once a tax lien is executed, interest on the lien is 14 percent per year under RSA 80:69.

Can I sell my Manchester house if there is a tax lien on it?

Yes. The lien is paid from the sale proceeds and released after payment, and the Tax Collector says a full redemption leads to a release within 30 days. Ask the Tax Collector for the current payoff before closing.

Who pays the New Hampshire transfer tax when a house sells?

Both sides do. The Department of Revenue Administration sets the rate at $0.75 per $100 of the price for each of the buyer and the seller, and transfers by will or intestate succession are exempt.

Where do I appeal a Manchester assessment after the Board of Assessors denies it?

File by September 1 with either the State Board of Tax and Land Appeals or Hillsborough County Superior Court, Northern District. You pick one, and choosing the state board waives the court option.

Where is Nashua and what does the city cover?

Nashua is a city in southern New Hampshire, right on the Massachusetts line in southeastern Hillsborough County. It shares the county seat role with Manchester.

The Census Bureau figures reproduced on Wikipedia give Nashua 31.73 square miles, of which 30.83 is land. The Merrimack River forms the eastern boundary, the Nashua River roughly cuts the city in two, and Pennichuck Brook marks the northern edge. The 2020 Census counted 91,322 residents, and a 2024 estimate puts the city at 91,851. There were 39,663 housing units in 2020, and 3.6 percent of them were vacant.

Several parts of the city have names that sellers and buyers use more than the official ward map:

  • Downtown, centered on Main Street and the Nashua River
  • French Hill in the north, which called itself Nashville during an 1842 split of the town
  • The Tree Streets neighborhood near downtown
  • The Amherst Street corridor (Route 101A) in the northwest
  • South Nashua along Daniel Webster Highway, next to the state line

What is Nashua's history?

The land was part of Dunstable, a Massachusetts tract first settled about 1654, and the New Hampshire half was renamed Nashua in 1836 after the river. Nashua became a city in 1853, after the town had split in two in 1842 and rejoined.

The Nashua Manufacturing Company was incorporated in 1823 and eventually ran four mills with about 1,000 workers. Six rail lines crossed the mill town. The mills prospered until about World War I, the 1922 New England textile strike shut them down for a time, and the last mill near Nashua closed in 1949.

The city's recovery started when Sanders Associates, a defense firm now part of BAE Systems, moved into a closed mill. Digital Equipment Corporation arrived in the 1970s. The city's housing today reflects both the mill era and the later technology decades.

What drives Nashua's economy?

Nashua's economy leans on professional services, high technology, defense, health care and retail. Wikipedia names BAE Systems, Dell and Oracle among the larger technology and defense names, and lists two hospitals, Southern New Hampshire Medical Center and St. Joseph Hospital.

The South Nashua commercial district, anchored by the Pheasant Lane Mall, draws Massachusetts shoppers because New Hampshire has no sales tax. Higher education includes Nashua Community College and Rivier University. The Boston Air Route Traffic Control Center is also in the city.

For sellers, the main effect is a buyer pool that includes commuters to the Boston area. The same Wikipedia page notes a Nashua-to-Boston bus line out of the Nashua Transit Center at Exit 8 of the Everett Turnpike, and the city has nine scheduled local bus routes.

How do Nashua's roads and weather affect a house here?

The Everett Turnpike is the main highway, with NH 101A, 111, 111A and 130 crossing the city. The Broad Street Parkway, finished in 2015, links Exit 6 of the turnpike to downtown.

Nashua winters are real. NOAA normals show a January daily mean of 24.1 degrees Fahrenheit, a July mean of 72.7, about 52.9 inches of snow a year, and 48.19 inches of precipitation. The city averages 26 to 30 days a year at 90 degrees or above.

MeasureValue
Elevation151 feet
Average annual snowfall52.9 inches
Average annual precipitation48.19 inches
Snowy days a year (0.1 inch or more)18.9
Days at or above 90 F26 to 30

With that much snow and rain, a roof, gutters and a basement are the first things to check before you list, or the first things a cash buyer will price in.

Who handles property tax in Nashua?

The Assessing Department sets values and the Tax Collector's Office bills and collects the tax. Both are at City Hall, 229 Main Street, Nashua, NH 03060.

The Assessing Department's phone is 603-589-3040, and its abatement desk is open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., closed 12:30 to 1:30 p.m. The Tax Collector's phone is 603-589-3190. Property tax mail goes to P.O. Box 885, Nashua, NH 03061, and the city says a mailed payment is on time if it is postmarked by the due date.

Payments can also be made online through the city's Pay Bills Online portal, by phone at 1-833-343-0229, at the counter, or in the secure drop box at the Elm Street entrance of City Hall. The city says starting with the first 2026 bills, taxpayers can view and download bills, payment history and balances online at any time. Nashua's Tax Collector lists accepted payment forms as cash, major credit cards, checks, money orders and bank checks.

What are Nashua's tax dates and recent rates?

Nashua's tax year runs April 1 to March 31, with two bills. The first is due July 1 and is an estimate based on 50 percent of the prior year's rate, and the second is due after the state sets the rate, generally no later than December 20.

The city's FAQ adds that when a home is bought or sold, property taxes are prorated by day from April 1. Late payments carry 8 percent interest, which matches RSA 76:13.

Tax yearRate per $1,000Note
2023$18.23Before the statistical revaluation
2024$15.90Down 12.8 percent; total value rose from $13.9 billion to $16.5 billion (18.7 percent)
2025$16.83Up 5.83 percent; bills mailed Nov. 14, due Dec. 15

These rates come from reports in the Nashua Telegraph, not from a city rate table, so check the city's Tax Rate History page for the figure that applies to your bill. The 2024 revaluation shows why a lower rate does not always mean a lower bill: values moved up at the same time.

How do you file an abatement in Nashua?

File a printed, signed application with the Assessing Department by March 1 after the notice of tax. The city says it accepts applications only after the final notice of tax is issued, and for the 2025 tax year the deadline was March 1, 2026.

The fillable online form does not submit anywhere. Print it, sign it, keep a copy, and hand-deliver it to 229 Main Street or mail it to P.O. Box 2019, Nashua, NH 03061. If you miss March 1, the city's FAQ says no action can be taken for the current tax year, although you can ask for a spring review for the following year. Appeals beyond the city go to the New Hampshire Board of Tax and Land Appeals.

If your name or address is wrong on the bill, the request has to be made in writing and signed by the owners, then faxed to 603-589-3079 or mailed to the Assessing Department. The Tax Collector cannot change it.

What if you sell a Nashua house and still get the tax bill?

The city says to forward the bill to the new owner, or send it back in the provided envelope with a note saying when you sold and to whom. A deed can take time to reach the Assessor, which is why bills sometimes arrive in the old owner's name.

Unpaid tax can become a lien under the state's collection law. RSA 80:69 sets interest at 14 percent per year on a recorded real estate tax lien, and the lien can be redeemed at any time before a deed is given by the collector.

  • Closing agents can request a final wastewater bill for a sale closing through a form on the city's Tax and Wastewater page.
  • Look up the account by its 8-digit parcel ID, found in the upper right corner of the bill.
  • The state transfer tax is $0.75 per $100 of the price, paid by both buyer and seller.

More questions about Nashua, NH Property Tax Guide

When are Nashua property tax bills due?

The first bill is due July 1 and the second is generally due no later than December 20, according to the city's FAQ. The 2025 second bills were mailed November 14 and due December 15.

What is the deadline to apply for a Nashua abatement?

March 1 after the notice of tax. Miss it and the city takes no action for that tax year, though you may ask for a spring review for the following year.

Are Nashua property taxes prorated when a house sells?

Yes. The city's FAQ says taxes are prorated by day from April 1 of that year when a home is bought or sold.

What interest does Nashua charge on late property tax?

8 percent. The city says mailed payments must be postmarked by the due date to avoid that interest charge.

Which county does Nashua's deed go to?

Hillsborough County. Deeds are recorded with the Hillsborough County Register of Deeds, and the transfer tax stamps are bought there, at $0.75 per $100 from each side.

Where is Concord, New Hampshire, and what does it cover?

Concord is the capital of New Hampshire and the seat of Merrimack County, in the south-central part of the state about 16 miles north of Manchester and 66 miles north of Boston. The city covers 67.2 square miles, of which 64 are land.

The Merrimack River runs northwest to southeast through the middle of the city. The Soucook River forms the eastern boundary with Pembroke, the Turkey River crosses the southwestern quarter, and the Contoocook River joins the Merrimack at Penacook. Penacook Lake, in the west, is the largest lake in the city and its main water source.

Property tax in Concord is a city, county and school matter, so the first thing to know is which part of the city your house is in. The villages are Penacook, Concord Heights, East Concord and West Concord, and downtown has its own North End and South End neighborhoods.

How does Concord's geography affect houses and taxes?

Downtown sits on a low terrace west of the river, while Concord Heights is a flat, sandy plain on top of a bluff about 100 feet above the Merrimack. Most of the city's commercial development since 1960 has been on the Heights. The highest point in the city is Oak Hill, at 860 feet.

Those landforms matter for a seller in practical ways.

  • Homes near the river and its tributaries should be checked against the FEMA flood map.
  • Penacook is served by the Merrimack Valley School District rather than the Concord School District, so the district you are in depends on where the house sits.
  • The Heights has seen most of the city's commercial development since 1960, so check what is nearby before you describe a location to buyers.

Concord's climate is humid continental, with about 42 inches of precipitation, about 67.7 inches of snow, and roughly 15 nights a year below zero. Roofs, heating systems and insulation get tested every winter.

Why does Concord's role as state capital matter to sellers?

Concord has been the official seat of New Hampshire government since 1808, and state government is a central part of the city's identity. The State House, completed in 1819, is the oldest U.S. state capitol where the legislature still meets in its original chambers. Concord became the Merrimack County seat in 1823.

The city also hosts the New Hampshire State Prison, the New Hampshire Police Academy and New Hampshire Fire Academy, NHTI, the University of New Hampshire School of Law and Concord Hospital, which opened in 1891 as Margaret Pillsbury General Hospital. A house sale still depends on the individual property.

When are Concord property tax bills due?

Concord bills twice a year and collects in four installments due July 1, October 1, January 2 and March 31. The July and October bills are estimates, each 25 percent of the prior year's total bill. The January and March payments are final and are adjusted for the earlier estimates.

The July and October bills are mailed together around June 1, and the January and March bills go out around December 1. Bills are based on the April 1 assessment under RSA 76:2. State law requires 8 percent interest on late balances, prorated daily, and the city cannot waive it.

ItemDetailSource
InstallmentsJuly 1, October 1, January 2, March 31City of Concord property tax page
Late interest8 percent, prorated dailyCity of Concord property tax page
Tax collector41 Green Street, 603-225-8540City of Concord property tax page
HoursMon, Tue, Wed, Fri 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM; Thu 8:00 AM to 6:00 PMCity of Concord property tax page
Assessing603-225-8550City of Concord abatement page

Payments can be made online, by phone, by mail to the City of Concord Tax Office, PO Box 9582, Manchester, NH 03108, or in person. Schedule mailed payments 7 to 10 days before the due date.

What is the Concord property tax rate?

The state's 2025 rate table lists Concord at $29.11 per $1,000 of assessed value. That total is made up of $10.18 for the city, $2.54 for the county, $1.58 for the state education tax and $14.81 for the local school district. The rate was set on November 19, 2025, on a valuation of $4,967,453,081 and a total commitment of $154,257,720.

On a house assessed at $400,000, that rate would produce a bill of about $11,644 a year. That is an illustration of the arithmetic only, and your own assessment decides your bill.

The largest piece is the local school rate. If your house is in Penacook or another part of the city, confirm your exact rate with the city assessor.

Is Concord reassessing property values?

Yes. Concord completed a citywide revaluation to bring assessments to full and true market value as of April 1, 2026. The New Hampshire Constitution requires values to be set anew at least once every five years, and the city's last revaluation was in 2021.

The city said new assessments would be announced in summer 2026 and finalized before the final 2026 tax bill in December 2026. Abatement applications are available in the Assessing office after December 1, 2026.

  • Compare your new assessment with recent sales of similar houses.
  • File an abatement application if you think the value is wrong.
  • If you are selling, expect a buyer to underwrite the new value rather than your old one.

How do I appeal a Concord assessment?

You apply to the city for an abatement by March 1 following the notice of tax. Under RSA 76:16, a person aggrieved by an assessment who has complied with RSA 74 may apply in writing by March 1, and the city must grant or deny in writing by July 1. A failure to respond counts as denial. The city lists March 1, 2027 as the deadline for the current cycle.

If the city denies your request, the denial letter must explain the next appeal step. Owners can go to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals or to superior court, and the Board's number is 603-271-2578. The state sets the abatement form, so use the current one from the city or the Board.

What happens if Concord property tax goes unpaid?

Unpaid tax can become a tax lien and, eventually, a tax deed, but the process takes at least two years. Under RSA 80:76, the collector executes a deed to the lienholder after 2 years from the execution of the lien if the land is not redeemed. At least 30 days before the deed, the collector must notify the owner under RSA 80:77 and mortgage holders under RSA 80:77-a, by certified mail.

The title company pays unpaid tax from your proceeds, so a sale while the lien is still redeemable resolves it. Because interest runs at 8 percent on late balances, waiting makes the payoff larger.

What transfer tax applies when selling in Concord?

New Hampshire's real estate transfer tax is $0.75 per $100 of the price, and it is imposed on both buyer and seller. The tax is filed and paid online through Granite Tax Connect, and the Department of Revenue Administration call center is 603-230-5920.

On a $400,000 sale, the tax is $3,000 per party, shown as an example only. Who bears the cost in practice is set by your purchase and sale agreement, so read the closing costs line carefully.

How do I sell a Concord house fast?

A cash sale is the shortest path to closing, and a listing may fit a house in good condition. A cash buyer takes a house as-is, so a Concord property with deferred roof work, tenants or a tax balance can still sell.

  • Get a payoff statement from your lender and a balance from the Tax Collector.
  • Find your 2026 assessment and compare it with your old one.
  • Request a written offer and check who pays each closing cost.

We buy Concord houses as-is and do not charge commission or fees to the seller.

More questions about Concord, NH Property Tax Guide

When are Concord property taxes due?

Concord's installments are due July 1, October 1, January 2 and March 31. July and October are estimates of 25 percent of the prior year's bill, and January and March are the final adjusted payments.

What is the Concord tax rate?

The state's 2025 rate table lists Concord at $29.11 per $1,000: $10.18 city, $2.54 county, $1.58 state education and $14.81 local school.

What is the interest on late Concord property tax?

The city says state law requires 8 percent interest, prorated daily, on balances past the due dates, and it cannot waive it.

What is the abatement deadline in Concord?

Under RSA 76:16, applications are due by March 1 after the notice of tax. The city lists March 1, 2027 for the current cycle, and forms are available in Assessing after December 1, 2026.

Can I sell a Concord house with unpaid taxes?

Yes. The unpaid tax and interest are paid from the closing proceeds. A tax deed cannot be issued until at least 2 years after the lien is executed, with 30 days of notice before the deed.

Who pays the New Hampshire transfer tax?

The tax is $0.75 per $100 and is imposed on both buyer and seller. Your purchase agreement sets how the cost is divided in practice.
